questions.q: Why was the author not hopeful that the Arab Spring would bring democracy?
options: The protesters were too few in number
Not quite. The article says: Democracy rests on education and institutions built beforehand, and these were lacking.
Democracy rests on education and institutions built beforehand, and these were lacking
Yes. He calls for a “pre-democracy revolution.”
Foreign powers would not allow elections
Not quite. The article says: Democracy rests on education and institutions built beforehand, and these were lacking.
Arab rulers were too popular to be replaced
Not quite. The article says: Democracy rests on education and institutions built beforehand, and these were lacking.
questions.rationale: “The base of democracy are institutions. Before establishing democracy we need to establish institutions and provide educational training. Without education, democracy is bound to turn into anarchy.”

questions.q: What does the article call “the spirit of democracy”?
options: The loser’s willing acceptance of defeat
Exactly. Without it, elections lead only to a “politics of opposition.”
Holding elections as often as possible
Not quite. The article says: The loser’s willing acceptance of defeat.
Removing a ruler by popular protest
Not quite. The article says: The loser’s willing acceptance of defeat.
Having many political parties
Not quite. The article says: The loser’s willing acceptance of defeat.
questions.rationale: “Acceptance of defeat is the spirit of democracy… the loser is the first to announce the acceptance of his defeat and sends his best wishes to the winner.”

questions.q: Mathematicians have called God a mathematician and Picasso called Him an artist. What does the article make of this?
options: Artists understand God better than scientists
Not quite. The article says: Each observer meets in the universe a mastery far beyond his own, and so recognises God’s greatness.
Each person imagines God in his own image, so none can be right
Not quite. The article says: Each observer meets in the universe a mastery far beyond his own, and so recognises God’s greatness.
God can be understood only through mathematics
Not quite. The article says: Each observer meets in the universe a mastery far beyond his own, and so recognises God’s greatness.
Each observer meets in the universe a mastery far beyond his own, and so recognises God’s greatness
Well read. God is the greatest mathematician, artist and genius.
questions.rationale: “One who observes the universe is confronted with the awesome feeling that there is a being greater than himself at work in it.”

questions.q: The article uses the statement “I am thirsty” as an example. What does it show?
options: A subjective statement can be valid if it stands rational scrutiny
Right. Thirst cannot be shown objectively, yet it is a real, natural need.
Subjective statements are always unreliable
Not quite. The article says: A subjective statement can be valid if it stands rational scrutiny.
Bodily needs matter more than spiritual ones
Not quite. The article says: A subjective statement can be valid if it stands rational scrutiny.
Only measurable needs are real
Not quite. The article says: A subjective statement can be valid if it stands rational scrutiny.
questions.rationale: “If it stands rational scrutiny, the subjective statement is as valid as the objective statement.” The article says the same holds for the natural urge to believe in God.

questions.q: A newspaper called Norway’s seed vault “a Noah’s Ark.” With whom does the article say it is better compared, and why?
options: Noah’s companions, who were saved by obedience
Not quite. The article says: Noah’s son, who trusted a mountain to save him from the flood.
The people of Mesopotamia, who stored grain
Not quite. The article says: Noah’s son, who trusted a mountain to save him from the flood.
Noah himself, who planned ahead
Not quite. The article says: Noah’s son, who trusted a mountain to save him from the flood.
Noah’s son, who trusted a mountain to save him from the flood
Yes. Noah told him no mountain could protect him from what God had sent.
questions.rationale: The son said, “I will betake myself for refuge to a mountain.” The article reads global warming as a warning that calls man to mend his ways, not merely to build shelters.

questions.q: When the Quraysh quarrelled over who should set the Black Stone in the Kabah wall, how did the young Muhammad settle it?
options: He gave the honour to the eldest man present
Not quite. The article says: He placed the stone on a sheet that all the leaders carried together, then set it in place himself.
He drew lots among the clans
Not quite. The article says: He placed the stone on a sheet that all the leaders carried together, then set it in place himself.
He placed the stone on a sheet that all the leaders carried together, then set it in place himself
Well done. Everyone took part and no one lost face.
He asked them to postpone the rebuilding
Not quite. The article says: He placed the stone on a sheet that all the leaders carried together, then set it in place himself.
questions.rationale: The article calls it “a fine example of how a controversial matter can be amicably solved, and to everyone’s entire satisfaction, by having everyone participate.”

questions.q: Which maxim does Dr Farida Khanam give for the position of men and women in Islam?
options: Equal in role, but different in respect
Not quite. The article says: Equal in respect, but different in role.
Equal in respect, but different in role
Correct. They complement, not duplicate, each other.
Alike in every sphere of life
Not quite. The article says: Equal in respect, but different in role.
Men first in public life, women first at home
Not quite. The article says: Equal in respect, but different in role.
questions.rationale: She likens them to a cart on two wheels: “Each of the wheels contributes equally to the running of the cart.”

questions.q: The article points to the rite of Sa‘i in Hajj, the running between Safa and Marwah. Why is it significant for the status of women?
options: It was introduced by the Prophet’s wife
Not quite. The article says: Every pilgrim follows in the footsteps of a woman, Hajira.
Women are excused from it out of respect
Not quite. The article says: Every pilgrim follows in the footsteps of a woman, Hajira.
Only women are required to perform it
Not quite. The article says: Every pilgrim follows in the footsteps of a woman, Hajira.
Every pilgrim follows in the footsteps of a woman, Hajira
Yes. The article sees no “better demonstration of a woman’s greatness.”
questions.rationale: “It is of the utmost significance that this was an act performed by a woman… God’s command to all men, literally to follow in her footsteps.”

questions.q: Why, in the author’s view, should we not expect the media to bring about social reform?
options: Journalists are poorly educated
Not quite. The article says: Media is an industry concerned with the present moment, while reform is a mission.
People no longer read newspapers
Not quite. The article says: Media is an industry concerned with the present moment, while reform is a mission.
Media is an industry concerned with the present moment, while reform is a mission
Exactly. He calls this an objective assessment, not a criticism.
Governments control what is printed
Not quite. The article says: Media is an industry concerned with the present moment, while reform is a mission.
questions.rationale: “Social reform is a mission, it cannot be a business.” Those who complain, he says, should “themselves start a mission for that purpose.”

questions.article: Religious Responses to the Troubles of Our Age
questions.q: Which two-point formula does the article give for a successful and peaceful life?
options: Demanding rights first, then performing duties
Not quite. The article says: Contentment in material things, idealism in spiritual things.
Contentment in material things, idealism in spiritual things
Right. Ideal justice is not achievable in a world of competition.
Protest against injustice, then patience
Not quite. The article says: Contentment in material things, idealism in spiritual things.
Idealism in material things, contentment in spiritual things
Not quite. The article says: Contentment in material things, idealism in spiritual things.
questions.rationale: “As regards material things, to remain contented, and in spiritual matters, to be idealistic… material ‘status quoism’ and spiritual idealism.”
